text: Boyd Crowder stood outside the church with a rocket launcher.
That was Boyd. He never did trouble small if he could make it loud. The church sat quiet in the dark, but Boyd had already made up his mind.
He raised the launcher and smiled.
"Fire in the hole."
Then he pulled the trigger.
The rocket hit, and the church blew open in fire and smoke. Wood cracked. Windows burst. The night lit up like judgment had fallen from the sky.
Boyd watched it burn.
To him, it was not just crime. It was a message. Boyd liked messages. He liked symbols, speeches, and anything that made men stare.
The men with him stared. Some looked pleased. Some looked scared. That was probably wise.
A man willing to fire a rocket into a church had already crossed more than one line. He had gone past anger. Past foolishness. Past ordinary lawbreaking.
Boyd lowered the launcher, and the fire behind him kept climbing.
The flames could be seen from far off.
People would talk. Police would come. Raylan would hear. Boyd knew that.
Maybe he wanted it.
Some men hide after they do wrong. Boyd liked to stand near the smoke and explain why he was right.
That made him dangerous, and it made him easy to find.
When Raylan heard the words, he knew.
"Fire in the hole."
That was not just a phrase to him. It came from the mines. It came from deep places, hard work, and men warning other men before the blast came.
Boyd had worked those mines too. Raylan did not need much more.

Raylan knew Boyd Crowder from before the badge and before the trouble got this big. They had been young men in the same hard country, working under the earth where coal dust got into a man's clothes and lungs.
That kind of past stays with you.
Boyd had gone one way. Raylan had gone another. But Raylan still knew how Boyd thought. Boyd wanted people watching. Boyd wanted to sound like a man with a cause, not just a man with a weapon.
That was part of the problem.
A fool with a gun was dangerous. Boyd was smarter than that.
Raylan heard about the church, the rocket, and the words shouted before the shot. He stood up.
Boyd had made it personal by being Boyd.
Raylan did not rush.
He checked his weapon, put on his hat, and let the old memories settle where they belonged.
Behind him.
Ahead of him was Boyd, an old friend, maybe. An old enemy, maybe. With Boyd, the line never stayed clean for long.
Raylan knew one thing. The next blast had to be stopped.
Raylan found Boyd where trouble usually found him.
Close to people. Close to talk. Close to a gun. Boyd smiled when he saw him, like Raylan had arrived for a visit instead of a reckoning.
Raylan did not smile back. He had heard Boyd's speeches before.
Boyd talked like he always did. Smooth. Clever. Too pleased with his own words. He talked about wrongs, old debts, broken systems, and men who needed to wake up.
Raylan listened with his hand loose near his side.
"You blew up a church, Boyd."
Boyd tilted his head, like the point needed more room. Raylan did not give it room.

Ava was nearby, and the air around the house felt tight. She had her own history with Boyd, and none of it was simple. Boyd was not just some stranger with wild eyes. He was a man who had stood too close to her life for too long.
That made the room smaller.
Boyd kept talking. Raylan kept watching his hands.
That was how Raylan worked.
Not much movement. Not much noise. He let the other man fill the air while he watched the part that mattered.
Boyd's words sounded calm. His body did not.
Raylan saw the shift. The little change before a man decides. The breath. The shoulder. The hand ready to prove what the mouth had been building.
Raylan said, "Don't."
Boyd heard him. Boyd moved anyway.
The draw came fast.
Boyd reached, and Raylan fired. One shot. Clean and hard. The room cracked with sound, and Boyd went down before his plan could become anything worse.
For a second, nobody moved.
That was how fast trouble can end when the right man is ready.
Raylan kept his gun on Boyd because alive did not mean harmless. Boyd was on the floor now, hurt and breathing, his big speech cut short.
The rocket was not here. The fire was not here. The crowd was not here.
Just Boyd, Raylan, and the choice Boyd had made.
Ava stood nearby, shaken but alive. That mattered.

Raylan had not come to make a legend. He had come to stop a man before more people got hurt. Sometimes stopping a man looked like handcuffs. Sometimes it looked like one fast shot before the other gun cleared leather.
Boyd had forced the moment. Raylan had finished it.
The sirens would come. The reports would be written. Men would talk about Boyd Crowder again, because Boyd always gave them something to talk about.
But Raylan knew the plain truth.
Boyd had shouted "fire in the hole" and sent a rocket into a church. Then he reached for a gun in Ava's house.
That was enough.
The fire was out. The law was still standing.
